text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth
as_written: eight minutes and twenty seconds
source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (astronomical unit = 149,597,870,700 m) divided by the speed of light, about 499 seconds; NASA

text: The sun is about 1.39 million km across
as_written: about one point three nine million kilometres across
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal solar radius of 695,700 km

text: The sun has been fusing hydrogen for about 4.6 billion years
as_written: about four point six billion years
source: Connelly et al. 2012, Science 338, dating of solar system solids; Bouvier and Wadhwa 2010, Nature Geoscience

text: Energy from the solar core takes roughly 10,000 to a couple of hundred thousand years to reach the surface, with the figure model dependent
as_written: from around ten thousand years to a couple of hundred thousand
source: Mitalas and Sills 1992, Astrophysical Journal 401; Stix 2003, Astronomische Nachrichten

text: The sun is about 149.6 million km from Earth
as_written: one hundred and forty-nine point six million kilometres
source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2, astronomical unit

text: Gravitational waves and gamma rays from the neutron star merger GW170817 arrived about 1.7 seconds apart
as_written: about one point seven seconds apart
source: LIGO, Virgo, Fermi GBM and INTEGRAL, 'Gravitational Waves and Gamma-rays from a Binary Neutron Star Merger', Astrophysical Journal Letters 848, L13, 2017

text: GW170817 was roughly 130 million light-years away, so the signals travelled about 130 million years
as_written: a journey of roughly one hundred and thirty million years
source: LIGO and Virgo, Physical Review Letters 119, 161101, 2017 (distance about 40 megaparsecs)

text: Earth's mean orbital speed is about 29.8 km/s
as_written: twenty-nine point eight kilometres every second
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet

text: The Moon reflects roughly 12 percent of the light that hits it
as_written: about twelve percent of what hits it
source: NASA Goddard Moon Fact Sheet (geometric albedo 0.12; Bond albedo about 0.11)

text: The sun and Moon each span about half a degree in the sky
as_written: about half a degree wide
source: NASA Goddard Sun and Moon Fact Sheets (angular diameters about 0.53 and 0.52 degrees)

text: The solar constant is about 1361 W per square metre
as_written: thirteen hundred and sixty-one watts
source: Kopp and Lean 2011, Geophysical Research Letters 38, L01706; NASA SORCE TIM

text: Globally averaged incoming sunlight is about 340 W per square metre
as_written: about three hundred and forty watts per square metre
source: Trenberth, Fasullo and Kiehl 2009, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society (340.4); NASA CERES

text: Earth emits about 240 W per square metre of infrared to space
as_written: roughly two hundred and forty watts per square metre
source: Trenberth, Fasullo and Kiehl 2009 (239); NASA CERES

text: The whole atmosphere holds about as much heat as the top few metres of the ocean
as_written: about as much heat as the top few metres of the ocean
source: NOAA Ocean Service and NASA Earth Observatory educational material on ocean heat capacity

text: Dry air is about 21 percent oxygen
as_written: about twenty-one percent oxygen
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet; NOAA

text: Total living biomass holds a tiny fraction of the carbon-equivalent oxygen in the atmosphere, so respiration and burning of all life would use only a small fraction of atmospheric oxygen
as_written: use only a small fraction of that oxygen
source: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS (biomass about 550 Gt carbon); Broecker 1970, Science, on oxygen reserves; own order-of-magnitude comparison

text: Marine phytoplankton turn over in days to weeks and account for roughly half of global photosynthesis
as_written: live for only days to weeks, and they carry out a huge share of all the photosynthesis on Earth, perhaps half
source: Field et al. 1998, Science 281 (ocean about 49 percent of net primary production); Behrenfeld and Falkowski 1997, Limnology and Oceanography

text: Global grain stocks cover a few months of use
as_written: Global grain stocks cover a few months of use
source: FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief (global cereal stocks-to-use ratio about 30 percent)

text: Humanity uses about 20 terawatts of primary energy
as_written: about twenty terawatts
source: Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy 2024 (about 620 exajoules in 2023, about 19.7 TW)

text: Earth intercepts about 174,000 terawatts of sunlight
as_written: about one hundred and seventy-four thousand terawatts
source: Derived: solar constant 1361 W per square metre times Earth's cross-section (NASA Earth Fact Sheet radius 6371 km)

text: Human energy use is well under 0.1 percent of the sunlight Earth intercepts
as_written: well under a tenth of one percent
source: Derived from the 20 TW and 174,000 TW figures above (about 0.011 percent)

text: Fossil fuels supply about 80 percent of world primary energy
as_written: about eighty percent of the world's primary energy
source: Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy 2024

text: Nuclear power produces about 9 percent of the world's electricity
as_written: about nine percent of the world's electricity
source: World Nuclear Association and IAEA PRIS

text: Reactors are refuelled on roughly 18 to 24 month cycles
as_written: eighteen to twenty-four months at a time
source: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission; World Nuclear Association

text: At the South Pole the sun sets around March and stays below the horizon for roughly six months
as_written: around March and does not rise again for roughly six months
source: US National Science Foundation, US Antarctic Program

text: About 90 percent of Icelandic homes are heated with geothermal hot water
as_written: about ninety percent of homes
source: Orkustofnun (Iceland National Energy Authority)

text: The lowest surface air temperature ever measured was minus 89.2 degrees Celsius at Vostok Station in July 1983
as_written: minus eighty-nine point two degrees Celsius, at Vostok Station in Antarctica, in July of 1983
source: World Meteorological Organization World Weather and Climate Extremes Archive

text: Large parts of the continents would reach record-cold temperatures within weeks to months of losing sunlight (estimate, explicitly flagged as uncertain)
as_written: within weeks to months, large parts of the continents would fall into that range
source: Energy-balance reasoning from the Trenberth et al. 2009 budget; flagged in the narration as an estimate, not a published model

text: The ocean's average depth is about 3,700 metres
as_written: about three thousand seven hundred metres deep
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (mean depth about 3,688 m)

text: Sea ice grows slowly and thickens by metres, not kilometres, in a year
as_written: it thickens by metres, not kilometres
source: Stefan ice-growth law applied with standard thermal constants; own order-of-magnitude estimate, not a published sunless-Earth model

text: The deep ocean sits only a few degrees above freezing
as_written: only a few degrees above freezing
source: NOAA Ocean Service

text: Earth's interior loses about 47 terawatts of heat
as_written: about forty-seven terawatts
source: Davies and Davies 2010, Solid Earth 1, 5-24

text: Average geothermal heat flux is roughly 0.09 W per square metre
as_written: nine hundredths of a watt per square metre
source: Davies and Davies 2010 (about 91 milliwatts per square metre); derived as 47 TW over Earth's surface area

text: Geothermal flux is nearly 4000 times weaker than average sunlight
as_written: nearly four thousand times weaker than the sun
source: Derived: 340 divided by about 0.09

text: No sunlight penetrates below about 1000 metres in the ocean
as_written: Below about a thousand metres, there has never been any sunlight at all
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, ocean light zones (aphotic zone)

text: Hydrothermal vent communities were found by Alvin on the Galápagos Rift in 1977, living on chemosynthesis
as_written: In 1977, the submersible Alvin dived on the Galápagos Rift
source: Corliss et al. 1979, Science 203, 1073-1083; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

text: Vent tube worms (Riftia) can grow taller than a person
as_written: tube worms taller than a person
source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (Riftia pachyptila up to about 2.4 m)

text: Deep subsurface life holds about 15 to 23 billion tonnes of carbon, hundreds of times the carbon mass of humans
as_written: between fifteen and twenty-three billion tonnes of carbon. That is hundreds of times the carbon in all human beings
source: Deep Carbon Observatory decadal report 2018; Magnabosco et al. 2018, Nature Geoscience 11, 707-717; Bar-On et al. 2018, PNAS (human biomass about 0.06 Gt carbon)

text: Nitrogen liquefies at about minus 196 degrees Celsius
as_written: minus one hundred and ninety-six degrees Celsius
source: NIST Chemistry WebBook (boiling point 77.36 K)

text: A bare planet radiating only 0.09 W per square metre would reach an equilibrium near 36 kelvin
as_written: about thirty-six kelvin
source: Own calculation from the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the Davies and Davies 2010 geothermal flux; flagged in the narration as a back-of-envelope estimate

text: Earth's orbital period is about 365.25 days
as_written: three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet

text: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4 degrees
as_written: twenty-three point four degrees
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet

text: The sun's tidal pull is a bit less than half the Moon's
as_written: a bit less than half the strength of the Moon's
source: NOAA National Ocean Service, tides and water levels (solar tide about 46 percent of lunar)

text: After Tambora's 1815 eruption, 1816 was the Year Without a Summer, with global cooling of roughly half a degree Celsius and crop failures in Europe and North America
as_written: Global temperatures dipped by only about half a degree Celsius
source: Raible et al. 2016, WIREs Climate Change 7, 569-589; Stothers 1984, Science 224

text: About 60 billion solar neutrinos pass through each square centimetre every second
as_written: About sixty billion solar neutrinos pass through every square centimetre
source: Bahcall, Serenelli and Basu 2005, Astrophysical Journal Letters 621; Borexino Collaboration 2018, Nature 562, 505-510

text: Solar neutrinos arrive in about the same 8 minutes and 20 seconds as light, and are detected by Borexino in Italy and Super-Kamiokande in Japan
as_written: Detectors on Earth, like Borexino in Italy and Super-Kamiokande in Japan
source: Borexino Collaboration 2018, Nature 562; Super-Kamiokande Collaboration, Physical Review D 94, 052010, 2016

text: Snowball Earth glaciations occurred around 700 million years ago and ended with volcanic carbon dioxide build-up
as_written: about seven hundred million years ago
source: Hoffman et al. 1998, Science 281, 1342-1346; Hoffman et al. 2017, Science Advances 3, e1600983

text: Fresh snow reflects roughly 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight
as_written: around eighty to ninety percent
source: US National Snow and Ice Data Center, albedo

text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds more than a million seed samples at about minus 18 degrees Celsius
as_written: more than a million seed samples from around the world sit in a vault kept at about minus eighteen degrees Celsius
source: Crop Trust and NordGen, Svalbard Global Seed Vault
